sections.h2: What closing costs does a Florida seller face?
sections.html:
The largest line printed in state law is documentary stamp tax on the deed, followed by recording charges, title work, and the seller's share of property taxes. Other items come from the sales contract, such as agent commissions, repair credits and association fees. Florida contracts leave many of these to negotiation, so the contract in front of you decides who pays what.

This page sticks to the charges that Florida statutes and the Department of Revenue set in writing. For anything else on your settlement statement, ask the title agent or closing attorney to explain the line before closing day.

sections.h2: How much is Florida documentary stamp tax on a deed?
sections.html:
The deed rate is 70 cents on each $100 of consideration, or portion of $100, in every county except Miami-Dade. Section 201.02 of the Florida Statutes states the 70 cent rate, and the Department of Revenue's page repeats it. Consideration is broader than cash: it includes money, the discharge of an obligation, and any mortgage or encumbrance on the property whether or not the buyer assumes it.

Miami-Dade County prints a different pair of numbers. The Department lists 60 cents per $100 plus a surtax of 45 cents per $100, and the surtax is not due on a document that transfers only a single-family dwelling. If your property sits in that county, ask the clerk's office which version applies to your deed.

The tax is paid to the county clerk when the deed is recorded. Deeds are taxable whether or not they are recorded, and a taxable document that never gets recorded is paid to the Department of Revenue instead. A certificate of title issued after a foreclosure sale is taxed on the highest and best bid at the sale under section 201.02(9), which matters to sellers whose lender is moving toward a sale date.

sections.h2: Who pays the doc stamps on a Florida sale?
sections.html:
The contract decides which side pays, but the state holds every party to the document liable. The Department of Revenue says all parties are liable for the tax regardless of which party agrees to pay it, and if one party is exempt, the tax must be paid by a non-exempt party.

No statute assigns the deed tax to the seller or the buyer, so read the closing cost paragraph of your contract. A seller who agreed to pay should expect the title agent to deduct the tax from proceeds at closing.

  • Taxable deeds listed by the Department: warranty, special warranty, quitclaim, trustee's and life estate deeds, plus deeds in lieu of foreclosure.
  • A personal representative's deed under a probated will is listed as not taxable.
  • Spousal homestead deeds where the only consideration is a mortgage, and divorce deeds for the marital home, are exempt under section 201.02(7).

sections.h2: What does the buyer's financing add?
sections.html:
Mortgages and notes carry stamp tax too. The Department prints 35 cents per $100 of the amount secured, and it says tax on a note is capped at $2,450 while mortgages have no cap. These charges attach to the buyer's loan, not the seller's deed, so a cash sale avoids them. The deed itself is a separate matter: because consideration counts any mortgage or encumbrance whether or not the buyer assumes it, a sale where the buyer takes the property subject to your existing loan still counts that debt in the deed tax base.

Ask the closing agent to show how the deed tax was figured on your statement, and compare the consideration line with your contract price.

A seller who still owes on a mortgage pays it off at closing from the sale proceeds, and the payoff figure comes from the lender. Ask the lender for a written payoff statement a few days before closing, because it changes daily as interest accrues.

The clerk's charges are set in section 28.24 of the Florida Statutes. The first page of an instrument up to 14 by 8.5 inches costs $5.00 and each added page costs $4.00. Each name beyond four adds $1.00. On top of that come a Public Records Modernization Trust Fund charge of $1.00 for the first page and $0.50 for each added page, and an additional $4 per page technology charge.

These are small beside the stamp tax. A deed that runs several pages with several grantors will cost more than a short one, so ask the closing agent for the recording total in advance.

sections.h2: Who pays for title insurance and what does it cover?
sections.html:
Title insurance rates are set through the Office of Insurance Regulation under a rule chapter called Title Insurance Rates, so the premium schedule comes from state rule. The history note on that rule cites sections 627.782 and 627.7825 of the Florida Statutes. Which side pays for the owner's policy is a contract term, so check the paragraph of your contract that covers title.

Section 627.7841 adds one protection that sellers should know about. When a title insurer's own officers, employees or agents disburse the closing funds, the insurer must cover adverse matters recorded between the commitment date and the recording of the deed, except matters the insured knows about. That is why closing through a title agent that handles the funds is routine in Florida.

sections.h2: How are property taxes and disclosures handled at closing?
sections.html:
Florida tax bills go out in November, and the Department of Revenue prints a discount of 4 percent in November, 3 in December, 2 in January and 1 in February. Unpaid taxes become delinquent on April 1. The closing agent usually prorates the year's tax between buyer and seller, and the contract states how. Ask the tax collector for the current bill if you do not have it.

Section 689.261 requires that a buyer of residential property receive a property tax disclosure summary at or before signing. It warns the buyer not to rely on the seller's current taxes, because a change of ownership or improvements triggers reassessment. The statute also says that beginning February 1, 2027, the current owner's taxes may not be printed in listing materials. That affects how your listing reads, so ask your agent how it will be presented.

faqs.q: Who normally pays documentary stamps in a Florida sale?
faqs.a: The contract decides, though the state holds all parties liable. The Department of Revenue says liability stays with every party to the document regardless of who agrees to pay. No statute names the payer, so the contract paragraph on closing costs controls between buyer and seller.

faqs.q: Does a cash buyer avoid the mortgage stamp tax?
faqs.a: Yes, because that tax attaches to mortgages and notes at 35 cents per $100 secured. A cash purchase has no new note, so only the deed tax and recording charges remain.
Yes. The Department of Revenue prints 60 cents per $100 plus a 45 cent surtax per $100 for Miami-Dade, and the surtax is not due on a document that transfers only a single-family dwelling.

faqs.q: What does it cost to record a deed?
faqs.a: The first page is $5.00 and each added page $4.00 under section 28.24, plus a trust fund charge and a $4 per page technology charge. Extra names beyond four add $1.00 each.

faqs.q: When are Florida property tax bills due?
faqs.a: Bills are sent in November, and unpaid taxes become delinquent on April 1. The early-payment discount runs from 4 percent in November down to 1 percent in February. Your closing agent handles the proration.
